notes.meaning: Joash became king as a small boy. He had been hidden in the temple for six years, so he was only about one year old when his aunt saved him from Athaliah's killings. Nothing more is known about his mother, Zibiah. Her name and home town were simply kept in the record.

Joash did right for as long as Jehoiada the priest lived. Jehoiada was a faithful adviser who guided him by God's word. The words "all the days of Jehoiada" quietly warn that things changed once Jehoiada died. Matthew Henry says it is a blessing for young people to have wise and good guides, and wise to listen to them.

Jehoiada chose two wives for the young king, acting like a father to him. Wicked queens like Jezebel and Athaliah had done great harm, so a careful choice mattered. Joash had sons and daughters, so David's royal family, which had nearly been wiped out, grew again.

Joash decided to repair the temple. Under the wicked rulers before him, it had been robbed to enrich the temple of Baal and left to fall apart. Matthew Henry says repairing places of worship is a good work that everyone should help with.

The king sent the priests and Levites (the temple helpers) to collect money from the towns of Judah. "All Israel" here means the people of Judah and Benjamin. The temple belonged to the whole nation, so it was right that everyone should help pay for it. Even so, the Levites were slow, perhaps from carelessness.

Joash asked Jehoiada why the money had not come in. Adam Clarke says the tax Moses set was the half-shekel each grown man paid, as in Exodus 30. Matthew Henry notes that the young king seemed more eager than the old priest. Henry adds that "it is easier to build temples than to be temples to God."

Here is the reason the temple needed repair. Athaliah's sons, urged on by her, broke into its treasures, damaged the building, and gave its holy objects to Baal worship. The Bible calls her wicked because she was a cruel murderer and worshiped idols.

The king had a chest made and set at the temple gate so people could drop in their gifts. Matthew Henry suggests that this new way of giving may itself have helped it work. Even willing givers need a clear way to give.

A public announcement called everyone to bring the gift Moses had set long ago in the wilderness. Gill compares it to the freewill gifts the people once gave for the tabernacle, the tent used for worship. The writer of Chronicles likes to stress that God's people gave willingly.

Leaders and people alike were glad to give, and they gave freely. Matthew Henry notes that much was given with great cheerfulness. Some explain the Hebrew as "until they had finished" giving, rather than "until the chest was full." Writers link this happy giving to "God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Whenever the chest held a lot of money, the Levites brought it in. The king's scribe and the high priest's officer emptied it and put it back. "Daily" means time after time, whenever it was full. Trusted men handled the money openly and honestly.

The king and Jehoiada passed the money to the work supervisors. They hired stonecutters, carpenters, and metalworkers. The king and the priest worked together, so it was done by shared counsel, not one man's wish. Matthew Henry praises the faithfulness of those who paid the money and those who did the work.
The work went well. The Hebrew uses a picture of healing, like a bandage laid on a wound. The temple was restored to its first plan, the designs of David and Solomon, and made strong again.

Money was left over, so new gold and silver vessels were made. They replaced the ones Athaliah and earlier wicked kings had taken or used for idols. Burnt offerings (sacrifices burned whole on the altar) were made regularly while Jehoiada lived. That phrase repeats verse 2 and marks the end of the good years.

Jehoiada died at 130, so he had been born in Solomon's time and lived through six reigns. Gill notes he lived longer than anyone recorded since Moses. His long life was a mercy to the king and the land.

Jehoiada was given a rare honor: burial among the kings in Jerusalem. He had done good for God and His temple, and in practice he had guided the kingdom. "Israel" here means Judah, the part of the nation still faithful to God. Matthew Henry says the greatest honor is to do good in our own time.

Once Jehoiada was gone, the leaders of Judah bowed before Joash and flattered him. They likely asked to worship at local shrines instead of traveling to Jerusalem, knowing idol worship could then go on unnoticed. Joash listened. Matthew Henry warns that faith must come from the heart, or we lose it when a godly guide is gone.

The people left God's temple and served idols, including Asherah poles (objects used to honor a false goddess). The same king and leaders who had repaired the temple now turned from it, which shows how changeable people are. God's anger came on them, and it soon showed itself in the Syrian invasion.
Even so, God in His mercy sent prophets to call the people back. He would rather sinners turn and live. The prophets solemnly warned of judgment, but the people would not listen.

God's Spirit came upon Zechariah, Jehoiada's son. The words literally mean the Spirit "clothed" him. He stood on raised ground in the temple court so all could hear him. Plainly and without harsh words, he reminded them of God's law: if you leave the Lord, you cannot prosper, and He will leave you.

At the king's order, they stoned Zechariah in the temple court. Matthew Henry calls it one of the worst crimes in the history of the kings. A priest and prophet was killed in a holy place for bringing God's message. Jesus later spoke of this Zechariah's murder in Matthew 23:35.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Matthew calls this Zechariah "son of Berechiah," and some modern writers think that is a slip by the Gospel writer or a mix-up with the later prophet Zechariah.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Many early Greek church fathers thought the Zechariah Jesus named was the father of John the Baptist.

notes.meaning: Joash forgot all the kindness Jehoiada had shown him and killed his son. There is a wordplay: Joash "did not remember," yet Zechariah's name means "the LORD remembers." As he died, Zechariah said the Lord would see and call Joash to account. Matthew Henry says this came from a spirit of prophecy, not revenge, and it soon came true.

Within about a year, the Syrian army, sent by King Hazael, invaded Judah and Jerusalem. They killed the leaders, the very men who had led the turn away from God. Wesley notes how quickly God answered the prophet's blood.

A small Syrian force beat Judah's huge army. When God's people stayed close to Him, they had often won against greater numbers. Now God was against them because they had left Him. The Syrians were God's tools to bring judgment on Joash, though they did not know it.

The Syrians left Joash badly wounded and sick. Then his own servants killed him in his bed because he had shed the blood of Jehoiada's son. He was buried in Jerusalem but not in the royal tombs. That was a mark of disgrace, in sharp contrast to Jehoiada's honored burial.

The two killers are named, and both had foreign mothers, one from Ammon and one from Moab. Matthew Henry thinks marriages like these, which God's law forbade to guard against idol worship, ended up bringing harm. The king, led astray by men who should have served him well, was killed by his own servants.

More about Joash was written in another record, which is now lost. The "pronouncements" about him likely mean the prophets' warnings against him, or God's heavy judgments on him. Some think instead that the word means the tribute he paid to Syria. His son Amaziah became king after him.
